utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, our screens are now working as well. General Galic, please remain seated. I checked yesterday about the flak jacket. And although this Chamber will not solve the problem, but I understood that proper attention is paid to it. And if finally there's no acceptable solution, then please come back with it to the Chamber. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you're standing, although cross-examination of Baron van Lynden was done by your colleague, so may I assume there's another issue you want to raise? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My learned colleague has a few more questions, so with your permission, I don't think we'll be overstepping our time limit. I think we have another 20 minutes. That's our assessment. And when my colleague concludes his questions, I shall continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps just as a matter of guidance to Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I noticed that quite frequently he repeats earlier answers given by the witness. And in our view, and since the Chamber may give you some directions as far as the examination of witnesses is concerned, I would do that only if there's really a necessity to bring back into the mind of the witness what he has said before. But very often, it's rather repetitious. So could you please keep that in mind, and of course you may proceed with the cross-examination of Mr. van Lynden. Mr. Usher, would you please bring him into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wait for one second, Mr. Usher. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to bother you at this point, but if the Defence proceeds with putting this letter which we provided him yesterday with because he couldn't print it out, we would like to object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could discuss it in the absence of the witness. Yes. You would object for what reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps Your Honours have seen the letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have not seen the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can briefly inform you that it's dated 19 January, 1993. It is a letter which has no bearing on the witness. It deals with an incident which happened in the afternoon of the 11th of January. And unless the Defence establishes that the witness was indeed there at the Kosevo hospital and that he had a sort of involvement with it, so he can confirm or deny, we would see no point in showing this letter to the witness. Also, the witness was asked whether -- in cross-examination, he was asked whether the Bosnian troops had used the hospital for military purposes, and his answer was no. Also, not in examination-in-chief or in his witness statement he pronounced on anything about the presence of a mortar on the grounds of the Kosevo hospital. So in our submission, we think it would not make sense to show the letter to this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor. I should like to note that the production of this document, that is to say, the letter and our wish to show it to the witness, has resulted in a certain amount of disquiet with the Prosecution. However, the letter indicates the fact that General Morillon, who is well versed in military skills, refers to a number of possibilities and says that it was possible that fire had been opened and that it was shelled from an area around Kosevo hospital. So it is indeed quite possible that this witness might have heard something about that. So if I ask him a few questions as to the contents of the letter, he might be able to give us some answers and respond. Furthermore, the Defence has always claimed that the press did not always report events accurately, and it is very important for this particular case to ascertain whether the press was well-informed and kept abreast of the actual events that took place. And this witness, who worked for one of the biggest world news agencies and for Sky News, satellite television, is precisely somebody well placed to be able to answer questions of that kind. So we think that is of substantive importance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. I think testing a journalist on the broadness of his information is part of testing the credibility of this witness and reliability of his knowledge. So you may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel. Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. van Lynden, the cross-examination by Defence counsel will now continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Baron, and thank you again for coming here. Can you hear me clearly? I believe you can with the interpretation. We stopped off yesterday discussing the Butmir situation, so let's take up where we left off. Is it true that you were provisionally detained, detained by the Bosniak authorities, while you were in the Butmir region? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that short, succinct answer. Is it also correct - I think that you said so - that you discussed the existence of a specific object at Butmir with certain Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, could you, in a word, specify what specific object that was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the tunnel that the Bosnians had dug from Dobrinja to Butmir, under the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Baron. Baron, is it also correct, if you have knowledge of that, or, rather, what was the attitude of the Bosnian authorities with respect to the existence of that tunnel when you asked them questions concerning the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attitude of those Bosnian authorities that I spoke to about the tunnel was either to deny its existence or to admit that it existed but not to let me anywhere near it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, see that I read well, you started questioning, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, on a detention caused by any discussion on the existence of a specific object at Butmir with certain Bosnian authorities. The answer then was -- "What was this object?" And then the answer reads:

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tunnel that the Bosnians had dug from Dobrinja to Butmir, under the airport. The Bosnians or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnians, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To go back to the tunnel that the Bosnians dug, Baron --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here the problem, in French you say, "the tunnel dug by Bosniaks."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript reads "the Bosnians."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I could say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the tunnel dug by the Bosnians or by the Bosniaks, just to use the words?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's a translation problem. So I - I do apologise, but "Bosniaks" mean "Bosnians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So sorry. So when I say "Bosniaks," it's "Bosnian." Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To go back to the tunnel, Baron, which was dug -- so the tunnel that was dug by the Bosnians, the people from Sarajevo, could you tell us, please, why they denied the existence of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's speculation on my part, but I would say the basic reasons were a question of security. As far as I'm aware, no journalists, foreign journalists or, for that matter, Bosnian journalists, were allowed anywhere near the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Baron. And when you say "security," use the term "security," am I correct in saying that you mean military security and strategic security?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a war zone, and therefore that's -- obviously they did not want their opponents to know of the existence, and if they knew of the existence, at least not of the precise existence of entrance and exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. The tunnel that was dug under the airport and which finished close to the Dobrinja zone, exited near the Dobrinja zone, was it also used to take through materiel, supplies, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no knowledge because I was never allowed anywhere near it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on to another area now, Baron van Lynden. With respect to the hospital, Kosevo hospital, first of all I have a question for you. When you saw the Kosevo building, the buildings, what physical state, condition, were they in? And I'm talking about the exterior walls, the whole Kosevo hospital complex.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw the Kosevo complex in May 1992. At that stage, there was some damage to some of the buildings. I went back to the complex which does exist of quite a number of buildings at different stages of the war, and the damage to the buildings had only increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Baron. Do you happen to know that there was a sports hall? Do you know about a sports hall which was called the Zetra, Z-E-T-R-A, close to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Baron. I should now like to show you a document, and I'm going to ask permission from the Chamber for the usher to help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, will you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to specify for the transcript that this is a document that we received from the set of documents from the Prosecution. It is ours. 0046717 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, with respect to that document which you have before you, and perhaps I could give you a few moments to peruse it, and then I shall be asking you some questions concerning the document. Have you had time to look through the document, Baron?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Baron, I apologise for repeating myself, but yesterday you said that you did not know that the Bosnian authorities had fired from Kosevo hospital. Is that right? In order to clarify this, we have a letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Already I think you explained extremely well what the letter is about. It's part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron, during your stay in Sarajevo, did you have an opportunity of meeting officials from the official press agency, the official Bosnian press agency? That is to say, did you attend press conferences organised by the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never attended a press conference organised by the Bosnian authorities, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Baron. However, you did indicate that you had direct contacts with the authorities, and we come to your answer with respect to the Butmir tunnel. Could you tell us at what level you had contacts of that kind?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had meetings with President Izetbegovic, Vice-President Arif Ganic. Later on with Prime Minister Silajdzic, and others working within the Bosnian Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Baron, for your answer. When you had these meetings at the highest level, did nobody ever say that hospitals had been used as a firing base by the Bosnian forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to remind my friend what he asked yesterday just before the break. His question: "Baron van Lynden, in your capacity of journalist this time, did you ever hear mentioned that at one point or another, and more specifically in the course of January 1993, that Bosnian troops had used a hospital for military purposes?" And the answer was no. And I wonder what this question would add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the objection. Thank you. Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, did you also have contacts with representatives of the UN authorities, the international organisations? And I'm referring specifically to the UN.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different parts of the UN in Sarajevo, but yes, I had contact with UNHCR and with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. And this brings me to my following question: Throughout your sojourn in the city, you received information from UNPROFOR in particular according to which the firing could have been done by Bosnians from civilian buildings?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a city is surrounded and you're defending a city, it is rather difficult not to fire from amongst its buildings, if those are the front lines. I mean, this argument never stood any ground with me. Nor did I ever, in my time in Sarajevo - and I was not in Sarajevo in January 1993 - ever receive a direct report from any UNPROFOR officer that the Bosnian authorities had used the Kosevo hospital as a military base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I was talking specifically about civilian buildings, but thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would -- perhaps this may assist you. Mr. van Lynden, you testified, and it has just been read to you yesterday, that you were not aware in your capacity as a journalist, although you are always answering questions in your capacity as a witness, that you didn't know anything about mortar fire fired from the Kosevo hospital. Now you say, "I had no direct report from any UNPROFOR." Did you have any indirect report?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I was just referring to the question, neither direct or indirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think we have any further questions regarding that letter as it stands for the moment. And as I said I would be brief, I am going to be brief, so that is all from me, and I'll give Ms. Pilipovic the chance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... subsequently, cross-examining the witness, I'll not make any objections since I do understand the problems the Defence may have in preparing the audiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to thank the Chamber profoundly, especially as I have already specified that for the coming witness, yet last night at 9.00 p.m., I received some changes to that -- related to that particular testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van Lynden, good morning. Yesterday, during your examination-in-chief, on line 11 at 9.16, you said that on the second or third day in Sarajevo, you visited the former military hospital and said that the hospital had been shelled. Could you please describe to us now what the condition of the hospital was when you arrived and saw it? And you did say that that was in May.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, indeed, in May, at the end of May 1992. The condition of the hospital was that certainly the top eight floors had all been wracked, both by gunfire, machine-gun, or rifle fire, and by heavier arms, including artillery shells of one nature or another. I can't specify what millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At 9.50 hours yesterday, and this time line 14, you told us that you were at Grbavica in a high-rise building where there were positions, as you said, of the army of Republika Srpska, and that that was in September. Could you tell us now, please, what high-rise building you were in in September? Or let me rephrase that: Could you describe the part of town you visited? Was it one high-rise or several?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken to several different apartment buildings, and they were in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which floor you were on in the building when you talked to the snipers and when you saw the dummy?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember, the dummy was on the fourth floor. I remember also being in one apartment on what I think was the second floor, a lower floor. And another building, we were higher up, fifth or sixth floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you visited the snipers and when you were on those floors, from those particular positions, could you see the positions of the army, the BH army?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In as far as I was personally able to sit by one of the positions and actually look out - one didn't do that for a great length of time - and I couldn't clearly see any of the positions of the Bosnian Army, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us at 9.55 hours, line 14, yesterday, and let me quote: "When we were in those buildings, I did not see anybody fire, but I heard the shooting." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, where you heard the shooting coming from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, within what sounded to us like within the building we were in, one shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear shooting coming from the other side? When I say, "the other side," I mean in respect to the side you were on, you were at?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in the apartment blocks, not. While we were in the streets of Grbavica before entering some of these buildings, yes, there was firing. But when we were in the buildings, I was not aware of any firing coming from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the streets at Grbavica, I think you said that, did you see any protection from the snipers that had been set up, along the streets that you passed by, any protection, barriers or whatever?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on occasion, much like on the other side, blankets had been hung down as a form of cover. As I remember, there were also some sandbag positions. But at that stage, I did not see what I saw later inside Sarajevo, which was the use of containers as protection against sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what those protective devices or covers or what it looked like? What was this made of? Because you said later on that containers were used. So could you describe to us what was used?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, blankets or tarpaulins were -- were hung down at various places but usually only in narrower streets where they could be held up on both sides so that people walking behind that would not be in the sight of snipers on the other side. This was done, as far as I'm aware, on both sides in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the time you spent at Grbavica, did you happen to learn whether that part of town had electricity and water?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were there, lights were on. So there was certainly electricity, yes. As far as water is concerned, I'm not aware. I don't -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday in line 18, at 10.09 hours, that the Serbs held the elevations and that they were able to fire at the central part of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could -- on the map that you used yesterday to answer my learned Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. friend's questions, could you draw in the positions, those positions, where they were, on the map you used yesterday, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way round Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as you know and with respect to the areas you were in.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using the black again?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, just to be sure, the answer of the witness was about the Serb-held elevations. That's not exactly posts. Do you want the witness to draw what would have been a front line or posts?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to have the witness show all the elevations for which he claims were held by the army of Republika Srpska. Could he indicate those positions on the map, the positions from which the Serbs fired at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think the testimony was that from Serb-held elevations that they were able to fire at a central part of Sarajevo. The testimony was not that they did at this and that spot fire but because they held these elevations that they were able to fire at the central part of Sarajevo. And I think you're now asking something given, which as far as I'm concerned is all right, but it's not a direct consequence of the answer given by the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may the witness be allowed to indicate the elevations on the map held by the Serbs around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want him to mark it, because that might be easy, or with great circles or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the witness could continue by drawing in larger circles and with the numbers, the ordinal numbers that he used when my colleague was asking the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please place the map on the ELMO so that we can all see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm going to draw, Your Honour, if I'm going to -- I mean, what they're asking for is a line all the way around Sarajevo. It's simpler for me to do it here and then put it under the light afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, the video will be kept in the archives. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whatever you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps -- would it really be necessary, Ms. Pilipovic? Couldn't the witness first indicate -- I mean, for example, just talking around Mount Trebevic, if he would point at that? We more or less know now where that is, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness could first indicate the hills and then, if necessary, mark it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer the question as to a rough drawing of the front line held by the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, if you would perhaps first tell us what elevations you are talking about, just giving the name and not marking them yet so that we will see whether we are acquainted with these hills or not and only if necessary to mark it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This entire area where my hand is now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How would you call that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is still part of Sarajevo and then it goes up onto Mount Trebevic, this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed with other elevations you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, these are the only ones that I ever visited or drove through. I was on the other side as well, but -- I'll turn the map around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that hill be known by any name to you, or these elevations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These elevations on the northern side, no. I don't have any precise names of hills there. I visited places like Vogosca, Krivoglavci I think it was called, Osijek where I saw Serb artillery, but of elevations and the names of those elevations, I don't have them, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, you may proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about Zuc hill yesterday. Can you indicate the location of Zuc hill on the map for us, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may mark it, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you draw a circle around it, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we were at number -- we haven't got the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six, Your Honour. I think the last I marked was five in black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would now be six then, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us yesterday that in 1992, in December to be precise, the Muslims forces took control of that particular hill. Do you know that BH army positions were on the hill?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken by the Bosnians rather than the Muslims, because there were also Serbs and Croats fighting in the Bosnian army, up onto Zuc hill, and I was shown their positions, yes. And those positions were still coming sporadically under mortar fire while I was up on that hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were at those positions, could you describe the part of Sarajevo that you could see from that area or, rather, can you see Sarajevo at all from those positions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Zuc you cannot, no, or at least I was not able to while I was up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From Zuc hill, were you able to see the environs of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The northern side to a degree, yes, but -- but you couldn't see the city proper, in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you were with members of the BH army at Zuc hill. Now I should like to ask you whether you visited any other positions of the BH army in that area. Did they take you to Hum hill?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not take me to Hum hill, as far as I'm aware. We were taken, as I said, to Zuc, and as far as I'm aware, I wasn't taken to other positions. I may have been taken to Hum hill. The name doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were at Trebevic. Can you mark in on the map which positions they were, Serb army positions that you visited?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with any precision at all. It was along the road that led from Pale to Lukavica, but I could not mark any precise positions on a map of this sort. No. But it was on the road, along the road, from Pale to Lukavica. So in this region.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That portion of the road that you used to go from Pale, would you consider that to be Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you consider that to be the foothills of Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never looked at it in detail in that manner, we just drove the road. Nor did we have any kind of map of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you were not at Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we took the road from Pale, and it went along Trebevic, as far as I'm aware, and it ended up -- the road ended up at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you were in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have been to the Lukavica barracks both in 1992 and in February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe to us what part of Sarajevo can be seen from the Lukavica barracks? What can you see from there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lukavica barracks is close to Dobrinja. As I remember, amongst the buildings, you couldn't see very much of Sarajevo from there. I mean, it was almost a front-line place, the front lines were very close. The Dobrinja front lines were very close, but you can't look down into the centre of the city from Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see the elevations in that part of the city in relation to Dobrinja from Lukavica? More specifically, could you see Mojmilo Brdo from that area?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, one could not. But I have to add that what one would do, one drove into the barracks. And it was not a place where you simply walked around freely. I mean, you parked your car by a building, and one went inside a building. One didn't wander around as one would as a tourist anywhere because, as I said, it was close to a front line. But as I -- as far as I can recall, I don't think that I could see Mojmilo hill. Maybe I could, but I don't recall being able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, were you, as a war correspondent, ever informed that the Mojmilo hill is an elevation near the Butmir airport and Dobrinja, and that the positions there were held throughout that period by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo, Mojmilo hill was held by the Serbs, by the Bosnian Serbs. It was only in June 1992 that I understand the Serb soldiers on Mojmilo were driven away by the Bosnian Army. I think I said yesterday, in relation to Dobrinja, that I went into Dobrinja, that that trip was only possible after the Bosnian Serb soldiers had left Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that in 1992, in June to be more specific, that combat had been going on at the Mojmilo hill between the BH army and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At line 11, at 11.06 hours --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to apologise if I'm not specific enough. I believe that this is the time. But let me remind the witness. He spoke about the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, that you spoke about the Marsal Tito barracks and about the Serbian army leaving the barracks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the time I did so, but I'm aware of speaking about the Marsal Tito barracks and the withdrawal of the Serb forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us at what -- when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it happened at the beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the barracks had been targeted by artillery. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the withdrawal of the forces, the Bosnian Serb forces from the Marsal Tito barracks, I saw several days of intense artillery and multiple rocket-launcher fire on the Marsal Tito barracks, yes. I saw this from the top floor of the former military hospital, now known as the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the positions from which the fire was opened on the barracks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see at a distance where artillery fire comes from, in my experience. So generally, the answer would be no. The only thing that we were able to see is that right on this side, right at the top of the mountain here, on the eastern side of Sarajevo, which was in view from the top floor of the hospital, you could see rocket fire emanating there and coming down on to the city. This is, I believe, the position that I was then taken to in September 1992 by General Mladic for the interview that I described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate to us on the map the position that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can do so only very roughly. It would be -- I imagine -- I don't know if the map goes far enough, but it was right at the top. The last -- it was, for us, the horizon. After that, there was sky. But it was visible directly from where I was in the centre of the city. The positions were somewhere up here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please make a mark and put in the number.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this area that you visited was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, the witness marked 7.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want the name, I take it, of where General Mladic took me to?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I was ever given a name. He never said, "I am taking you to there and there." He just took us along.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you later, during your stay in Sarajevo, learn what this area was called? Because you told us that artillery fire had been opened from that area.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your stay in Sarajevo, were you able to see that the Marsal Tito barracks was attacked by the territorial defence which, as you have said, existed at the time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there was shooting between territorial defence or other Bosnians and those inside the Marsal Tito barracks. But I never at that time actually saw people shooting. By the time -- during the time that I was in the hospital, I never directly witnessed fire going from either one side or the other. But I heard from a distance, but I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo as a war correspondent, did you have any contacts or do you have any knowledge of the existence of paramilitary formations in Sarajevo? Let me remind you, I'm speaking about Musan Topalovic, Caco; Ismet Bajramovic, Celo; and Juka Prazina. Did you hear about that and did you have any contacts with these people?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of them. And I met Juka Prazina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge as to where the headquarters of his force was located and how many people there were in this unit?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did go to one building. If it was his headquarters, I don't know, but that's certainly where I met him on several occasions. How many men? And this is, Your Honour, in May and June 1992. I had no further contact with Mr. Prazina when I returned to Sarajevo in the autumn of 1992 or thereafter, but in the May, June, and July period, I did. I went to one building where I met him on two or three occasions, and as far as I am aware, although he never actually gave a figure, there were maybe 200 or 300 men working under his command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe to us the uniform or, rather, what Mr. Prazina, to whom you spoke, was dressed; and if you had seen any of his soldiers, did they have any particular insignia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I met Mr. Prazina, he was wearing jeans and a T-shirt, and he had been fairly severely wounded, and he had external fixators, as I remember, at the top of his left arm and at the top of his left leg. He was not wearing a uniform, and it was inside the building. Nor did his men, as I -- as I can recall now, in the initial stages when I encountered them, wear any particular uniform. Later on, many of them were clad in black overalls. I don't remember any insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were, as you said, a paramilitary organisation; therefore, they had arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how important it is for a war correspondent to be objective and impartial? I mean, personal impartiality, how important is it, according to you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that any journalist doing any kind of job strives to be as objective as possible in the work that he does and to be as accurate as possible, as he can be, in the work that he does.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your career, has it ever happened that an agency that you worked for refused to publish your report in its original form?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your stay in Sarajevo as a war correspondent, were you informed that there were prisons in Sarajevo? Did you know what these locations were?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were aware that there were prisons. We also asked the Bosnian authorities if we could have access to these prisons in Sarajevo. We were never given access. In other parts within Bosnia held by the Bosnian authorities, we were given access. But I don't know, as far as Sarajevo is concerned, any precise locations of the prisons, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you identify the locations? Could you tell us which locations you went to that you said were prisons and that the Bosnian authorities allowed you to visit?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February 1993, I walked through Serb lines into the enclave of Gorazde and there we were taken into a prison, filmed and interviewed the Serb -- Bosnian Serb prisoners held there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you are questioning the witness now in relation to prisons. I think prisons have not been part of the examination-in-chief. I do not see at this moment, but please clarify this to me if I'm mistaken, any credibility aspect as far as prisons are concerned. So if it is the third part of Rule 90(H) which --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Since the witness spent quite a long time in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then you have to explain to the witness what the case of the Defence is in this respect. So at first you have to indicate what the case of the Defence is in relation to prisons and then you may put questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence, of course, understands the Rule 90(H). My question for this witness will be whether it is correct that there were prisons for Serbs in Sarajevo and that these prisons were located in the Viktor Bubanj barracks in Silos and in Tarcin and if he had any knowledge of the existence of these prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question about prisons in Sarajevo has been asked, but you continued talking about prisons elsewhere, because the witness said -- his testimony was that he was not aware of location of prisons in Sarajevo, that he had never access although he had requested to get access, but he never had access to these prisons. So if you are -- first of all, I do not see in your pre-trial brief anything about prisons, as far as I remember, but there again, my memory may not be good enough. But I do not see what prisons outside Sarajevo - as you just indicated to us that the case of the Prosecution was about prisons within Sarajevo - how they could be relevant for the case of the Prosecution -- for the case of the Defence. Would you please -- Mr. Ierace, would you intervene? You may make the observations you intend to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I only seek to assist by observing that the wording of Rule 90(H) requires the Defence in this case, that is, the cross-examining party, to put the nature of that party's case to the witness only when it is in contradiction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's the second requirement. But since I didn't see at all at this moment that this was relevant to the case, but I do agree with you that I don't see any contradiction at this moment. So, Ms. Pilipovic, apart from the contradiction aspect, also on the other aspect that the relevance for the case of the Defence, as you just explained it to us, doesn't seem to be there as far as I'm right in understanding your questions, your case, and the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question asked by the Defence will be rephrased in such a way that I will just ask the witness whether he knew that there was a prison in the Viktor Bubanj barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he already answered the question that he was not aware of any specific location. I think the question was repetitious unless the witness now says he was mistaken and, hearing this name, he would testify different. I would say that I'll not allow this repetition of questions. Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question has not been put to the witness but nevertheless answered. You may proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about being at the VRS positions, could you please tell me, what weapons did you see there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which positions are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the VRS positions that you said you had visited. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited a lot of VRS positions. I mean, on the mountain, it was a different thing. On the hills, it was a different thing to inside the city. Inside the city, I saw Kalashnikovs, sniper rifles, heavy machine-guns and, behind buildings, tanks, armoured personnel carriers with machine-guns mounted on top and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't finished. And anti-aircraft guns mounted on vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me in what part of the town did you see anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Grbavica and Hrasno.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, did you visit Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified yesterday that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us on the map the location that you claim you had visited and that you claim is, in fact, Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm marking it with an 8, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, did you visit the Pere Kosorica Square in Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any of the names of either the streets or the squares that I visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Hrasno is adjacent to what part of the town?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of the fact that, throughout the conflict in Sarajevo, Hrasno was controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of the fact that the Pere Kosorica Square was the line of demarcation between Hrasno and Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've already said, I don't know the names of either the streets or squares.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you visit Hrasno during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: He has testified several times that he has been there, in his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to Grbavica, could you draw in the confrontation line, looking at Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line that you already see here is the rough line that I recollect as being the front lines in this area. This is very rough, and I'm -- that's as far as I can generally say that the front line went.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Before -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It is obvious that what we saw being produced under D27, the letter that we tendered to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have spoken too quickly when I said that this was evidence already since it still had to be admitted into evidence. The objection raised has been denied. Is there any other objection? Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We object. There is no relevancy of this letter to the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll decide on that after the break. And the number will be D28, if admitted into evidence, because D28 is the next number, as far as the Registry tells me. Is there any -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we would also like to tender the actual statement of the witness that he referred to during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked at all occasions that the lines would be read to him. And we earlier decided that the previous statements as a whole, especially when they are not covered by the examination-in-chief or by the cross-examination, would not be admitted into evidence. This would be an introduction of previous statements which we --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was just conferring with my counsel. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any need for re-examination, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, you said in answering one of the questions by the Defence that Serbs and Croats were in the Bosnian Army alongside the Muslims. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I met Serbs and Croats fighting in the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. So this concludes the examination -- yes, of course. I have forgotten to ask my colleagues whether they have any additional questions. My apologies. Judge Nieto-Navia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You described the protection used in Sarajevo, the protection from snipers; blankets and containers and so on. Did you see any similar protection or something used by the Serbs in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was put by the Defence attorney, and my answer was yes. Not containers. In 1992, I did not see the use of containers. I did see the use of tarpaulins, blankets, and such. This is usually in fairly narrow streets so it can be connected by both sides of two walls to be hung up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. And there was a question yesterday about the civilian victims on the Serb side. And you said, as far as I understood, that you never saw civilian victims there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We asked to be taken to a hospital or to a clinic, but we were never taken on the -- those parts of Sarajevo held by the Bosnian Serbs. They informed us that they had had civilian casualties, but I never personally saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Did you see civilian casualties on the other side, I mean in Sarajevo, in the city?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did; very many. Because as I've also explained to the Court, our base every night in Sarajevo when inside the city was the former military, now the State Hospital. And I saw a lot of civilians being brought into that hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I might have one question to you as well. You have told this Court about sniping from both sides. Can you make an assessment of how intensive it was, one side compared to the other side? Was it more intensive on one side, was it more intensive on the other side, or was it equal? Could you please try to give an assessment of that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try, Your Honour, but I have to immediately say that I was there with one television team, and I didn't have the kind of possibilities to view it as an UNPROFOR commander would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I do not ask for any statistical analysis, but what was your impression? And if you say, "I couldn't possibly answer the question," please tell me.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, my impression, our impression was that there was always far greater capability on the Bosnian Serb side than on the Bosnian side. Every type of weaponry was in demand in -- and there was a shortage on the Bosnian side, and there was a clear predominance on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're now talking about all the weaponry. As far as sniping is concerned, is this true as well?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're talking about the capacity, the capability of doing things. Is that a theoretical assessment of capacity or was it what you actually experienced while being there, by hearing, seeing?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what we heard and saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. van Lynden -- yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to ask that four Prosecution exhibits be introduced into evidence at the conclusion of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are now at the conclusion. We can deal with that, I think, right away. Madam Registrar -- let me just try and see. I think we started with the black and white map 3644VL. That's the map as it has been marked by Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I also have 3647A, which is the footing that goes with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the transcript of the footing of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be -- Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3647A is the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the Bosnian translation P3647A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we've got now three exhibits and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the video itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the video itself. And that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P3647.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -47. Then these exhibits are put into evidence. Then we have D28 for the Defence, as far as I am aware of. That's the letter of General Morillon. Yes. We had your objection, but it's -- I think it had been admitted already in evidence, or at least, it is now. So this concludes the examination of Mr. van Lynden. Thank you very much for coming. Usually I say to the witnesses "having come so far," but I've got no idea how far you have come, but nevertheless, this Court is grateful that you gave us the information asked by the parties but of importance for the decisions to be taken by this Court. Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, would you please lead Mr. van Lynden out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I indicated yesterday, after the examination of Mr. van Lynden, we'll just spend some time on the motion still pending, but I think it should be done in closed session because there is some confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before that occurs, Mr. President, might I respectfully request that that oral argument take place after the break? I need to speak to one of my colleagues to obtain some further information. However, yesterday, Mr. President, you also reminded the Prosecution of the requirement of the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution submit a draft scenario so as to reduce the Prosecution case in a way by which it will finish by early July. Mr. President, if it is acceptable that the argument in relation to videolink occur after the break, could I use the remaining five minutes to say something in relation to the request by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. I wish to make a few observations that may assist all of us in achieving a faster trial. I commence with the paper, Mr. President, that you handed down last week in which you calculated that the estimate of the Prosecution case was now some 975 hours, which would take us until March of next year. I note that the manner in which you arrived at that conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The arithmetics. I'm quite convinced some criticism could be done about. It was just confrontative. So I'm not that much interested in whether there are any smaller or bigger mistakes in that. It is just to confront you that it might end this way, and I would rather not make this calculation part of the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's not my point, Mr. President, I assure you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I simply made the observation that it's based on the witnesses we have heard so far. It may assist the Trial Chamber if I explain the structure of the Prosecution case. Effectively, it is divided four ways, that is, four discrete segments. The first segment is what we had described as overview witnesses. The next witness will be the last witness of that segment, that is, the last overview witness. There are one or two witnesses who will emerge later in the trial who perhaps could be characterised in that way, but essentially that will be it for overview. The second phase comprises witnesses who will give evidence in relation to the scheduled sniping incidents. The third phase, the witnesses in relation to the scheduled shelling incidents. The fourth phase one could characterise as international witnesses such as UNPROFOR officials, UNMOs, and the like. The relevance of the fourth phase is in a large part to the command and control aspect of the accused. So the reason I raise that estimate of 975 hours is simply that I do not anticipate that the witnesses in the second and third phase will take anything like the average period of time that the overview witnesses have taken, particularly with the use of the video and 360 degree photographs. So, Mr. President, that's the first observation I make. Secondly, the Prosecution, on the 25th of November last year, wrote to the Defence and informed the Defence that as a result of pressure from the Pre-Trial Chamber at that stage of proceedings, the Defence -- the Prosecution proposed to call -- to put before the Trial Chamber evidence of 32 witnesses in the form of 92 bis -- Rule 92 bis statements. The Defence responded to that by way of a formal filing in which it opposed the giving of evidence in that fashion by all of the 32 witnesses. A mission has taken place to obtain the statements of those 32 witnesses, or at least those who reside in Sarajevo. That mission was completed last week. I anticipate that the statements will be provided to the Defence by tomorrow, and they then have seven days to formally state their objection. In other words, within a week, the Trial Chamber will be in a position to make a ruling on whether approximately 30 witnesses will be able to give their evidence by 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I just may comment on that. As you have seen from my calculation, I started with 150 viva voce witnesses. That means that I anticipated already to some extent that perhaps not all the witnesses would be called or that there would be 92 bis witnesses. So I don't know. Do you anticipate that the number of 150 would be considerably lower, or...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the calculation assumes that the Prosecution succeeds in having the witnesses it proposes to be called by way of 92 bis in fact called -- their evidence given in that fashion. But we don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree that, in your scenario, of course, you are still facing some uncertainties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. My next point, Mr. President and Your Honours, is this: There have now been a number of occasions in which we have discussed the application of Rule 90(H)(ii) to the cross-examination by the Defence of Prosecution witnesses. Essentially, on the one hand, in its pre-trial brief, the Defence has said, in effect, that the accused denies that any of the forces under his command or control deliberately or recklessly sniped and shelled civilians. If that happened, he didn't know about it. On the other hand, we have had witness after witness who has given eyewitness and hearsay accounts of precisely that behaviour. And not once has it been put to those witnesses, as is required by Rule 90(H)(ii), that the evidence is inconsistent with the Defence case. Now, Mr. President, given the request that you made of the Prosecution last week, that does place us in a dilemma. On the face of Rule 90, we are entitled to conclude that no part of the evidence so far called is inconsistent with the Defence case with the exception of whether SRK artillery units deployed the technique known as the "iron cross." That, in my recollection, is the only aspect of the relevant evidence which has even been questioned, and even that was not squarely challenged. On the other hand, we have the Defence pre-trial brief whereupon the evidence which has been called so far is challenged. In order to tailor our case, we must have regard to what is still in issue. And as I've said, we could rely on Rule 90 except for the existence of the Defence pre-trial brief. That to one side, the fact that evidence is not contradicted, does not, of course, mean that it will be accepted by you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We still have a burden to discharge to satisfy you on the basis of credible evidence of the facts that we seek to prove. Mr. President, it seems to me that the Prosecution is entitled to take into account the attitude of the Defence to the evidence we have so far called in spite of its pre-trial brief, but I would be grateful if Your Honours and you, Mr. President, could provide us with some guidance in relation to the contradiction of Rule 90 and the contents of the Defence pre-trial brief. My final point is this: I am grateful that in particular over the last few days, as the Prosecution has led its witnesses to the relevant portions, that is, the portions of evidence that one might suspect would be in dispute, there has been little objection by the Defence to that form of eliciting evidence. I propose to continue in that fashion, that is, to use leading until such time that the Defence objects, so that we can get quickly to the relevant issues. Mr. President and Your Honours, by way of conclusion, one suspects, having regard to the conduct of the Defence in its cross-examination, almost by a process of elimination, that the Defence does not dispute that there was widespread and systematic shelling and sniping of civilians during the course of the tenure of the accused on the Bosniak side of the confrontation line perpetrated by forces on the SRK side of the confrontation line. One, perhaps, concludes that the real issue here is the issue of command and control. One wonders whether, in effect, the Defence has abandoned the first arm of my summary of the Defence pre-trial brief. In other words --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I have a problem with the interpretation in French that I am listening to. I don't know whether it was said "Bosnian" or "Bosniak."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Bosniak. Could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. You are not questioning the Prosecution. You said it was a translation problem. Mr. Ierace responded to that. Please continue, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That really does conclude my observations and my request for some assistance in relation to one aspect. Could I respectfully submit that, since we are about to embark on the second phase of the Prosecution case, that we wait until we have a judgement on the 92 bis application. By then, we would have had a week of the scheduled sniping incident evidence, and we may have a better idea as to how the -- how much time that evidence is likely to take. In other words, we may have an idea as to whether, as I anticipate, the Prosecution case does significantly accelerate. Overview witnesses, by their nature, are lengthy. They have much to say on many aspects of relevant evidence. The same does not apply for scheduled sniping incident witnesses, with one proviso. Many of those witnesses are in a position to give evidence about unscheduled sniping and shelling as well. Depending on what, if anything, Your Honours say by way of response to my request, it may be that the Prosecution does not call from those witnesses the evidence which they are in a position to give of unscheduled shelling and sniping incidents. In other words, the Prosecution may, in that circumstance, be satisfied with the evidence of the scheduled incident. Mr. President and Your Honours, of course, in making these comments, I am mindful that there is jurisprudence in the Tribunal that schedules to an indictment are part of the indictment. In other words, it is not easy for the Prosecution to not call evidence in relation to those incidents. Of the 27 or 26 scheduled incidents, we have some 40-odd witnesses, slightly over 40, I think, in a position to give viva voce evidence. So there is a limitation on what we can do. If one assumes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that there are 22 weeks, say 20 weeks, of evidence between the 1st of February and the beginning of July, taking into account -- that takes into account ten days for breaks and holidays, then I think one arrives at a figure of some 400 hours of evidence. And that's based on the realistic four hours per day, not four and a half. If one, then, divides that by two, to allow for cross-examination time, that would leave the Prosecution with 200 hours in which to conduct its examination-in-chief of its remaining 150 witnesses, which I think, on my rough mathematics, leaves something like one and a quarter hours per witness. Even with a speedy remaining Prosecution case, that may be a little bit unrealistic. But on the other hand, we may be able to get very close to it if, indeed, we move quickly through the sniping phase. And next week should bear that out. The first incident that I will call evidence in respect of will be a little longer than the average if I go beyond the evidence strictly in relation to the scheduled sniping incident. But even so, I don't expect it will be anything like the average of the overview witnesses. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think your observations are giving us something to think about. And since we have a break anyhow at this moment, we'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 11.00. We'll give proper thought to your observations and might not come back to it right after the break. After the break, when we start at 10 minutes past 11.00, we would like to have oral argument, but brief argument. Especially the Chamber has some additional questions to the motion. And we then start in closed session because of the confidentiality. And it's not my intention that if the parties would like to make any additional observations apart from the questions the Chamber may have, I would really limit that to 5 minutes each party, not more. I think the most important things can be said, roughly outlined, in 5 minutes. If then there's any additional time needed, just let us know, and we can decide on whether we will grant you some extra time. So we'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a couple of words, and I do apologise. This has now become a litany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we are now in open session again. It is not relating to the motion, but is a part of your litany, as far as I understand? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to indicate, whether we are in private session or open session, this is, Mr. President, just to say that, in relation to the witness who is about to appear, it was only yesterday that we received, at 21.00 hours by fax, additional statements or parts of additional statements that were modifying or adding new elements to the previous statement. So it was really not possible to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you please inform the Chamber about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what exactly it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. President. I'm grateful to the opportunity because it's an issue which has been alluded to by my friend in the past. Mr. President, in the course of briefing a witness who travels to The Hague to give evidence, it often occurs that further relevant information is provided by the witness to an investigator or a trial lawyer which was not previously known to us. By "relevant information," I mean information which is either relevant to our reciprocal disclosure obligations or Rule 68 exculpatory material or material which the Prosecution may want to use. It is important if the Prosecution learns such information, even at the last minute, that it makes the Defence aware of it. We choose to do that in writing so that the Defence may have no complaint as to the detail of that last-minute information. That is what my friend is referring to. For convenience, I describe the sheets that contain this information as supplementary information sheets; therefore, the Defence does not receive such a sheet in relation to all witnesses. Many of those witnesses where we have last-minute relevant information which they would want to know about, by its nature, it will be the day before or the morning of the witness giving the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. I do understand it's last-minute information. Of course, the question is whether it should have been last-minute information or whether it could have been obtained at an earlier stage. So we cannot assess at this moment. We'll see what happens. And if at a certain moment this additional information, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is such that you feel, apart from the general part of your litany but more specifically, that you have not had a good opportunity to prepare for cross-examination of the witness, then of course, please indicate to us. And if you then need additional time with General Galic, then please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that we are going to proceed differently, if you'll allow us. I noted the reference that my learned colleague, Mr. Ierace, made to Rule 68. And this is specifically about the exculpatory material in respect of General Galic, and I thank you for this submission. And we shall see how we will have this explained to us, these conditions, in which respect of these elements are exculpatory to General Galic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see that. The reference has been made to Rule 68, so we'll see how this works out. Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the next witness. Who is going to examine the witness, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will examine the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least you are replying, so I do assume you can hear me in a language you understand. Mr. Hvaal, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I'm hearing the wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then, please -- I think Channel 4. This is no commercial, but Channel 4 is the right one I think. Yes? The rules require you to make a solemn declaration at the beginning of your testimony, Mr. Hvaal. The text will be handed out to you by the usher. Would you please make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll first be examined by the Prosecution who called you as a witness. Mr. Ierace, proceed. And you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Morten Hvaal, spelled H-V-A-A-L?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you born and educated in Norway?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you a photojournalist by occupation?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the last 16 years, have you covered numerous armed conflicts throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Since 1982, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And were those conflicts in many countries, including the former Yugoslavia, various states in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And, of course, Europe. Did you first travel to Sarajevo during the armed conflict in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you stay there a short while and then return in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you essentially, thereafter, stay in Sarajevo until sometime in 1997?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Yes, with breaks. But I was basically based in Sarajevo for that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to breaks, between September 1992 and August 1994, were you ever away from Sarajevo for a period of longer than a month?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL
utterances.text: Perhaps on a few occasions, but not more than six weeks to two months ever, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
